newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU avoids defining recession in EMU pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU avoids defining recession in EMU pact.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday left unspecified the economic conditions under which a country joining a common European currency could run excessive deficits without facing stiff penalties.

Speaking at a news conference, Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said the maximum fine the Commission could impose on EMU members with excessive budget deficits would be 0.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
After intense negotiations, however, the Commission shied away from quantifying the extent of an economic downturn which would essentially let a government off the hook.

Instead, de Silguy said that the circumstances in each country would have to be analysed and that therefore differences between countries precluded putting exact figures on what constituted a severe recession.

So-called budget stability is considered an essential feature of economic and monetary union (EMU), designed to ensure budgetary discipline among governments joining a single currency, expected in 1999.
Officials said there was strong resistance from several southern European countries to an explicit definition of a severe recession.
De Silguy initially advocated defining such exceptional circumstances as negative real GDP growth of 1.5 percent for a full year.

The Commission also proposed an initial fine of 0.2 percent of GDP for EMU members running excessive deficits and that an additional 0.1 percent of GDP would be levied as a fine for every percentage point by which a country exceeds the three percent Maastricht threshold.
The proposed stability pact will be discussed by European Finance Ministers in the coming weeks with a final agreement expected by the time of the summit of EU leaders in Dublin in December.
